triage_context.environment: Internet-facing web service (HTTP is untrusted). identity-api, webapp and mobile-bff have external endpoints in the Aspire AppHost; the other services are internal and reachable through the BFF or after a service compromise.
triage_context.votes_policy: 3 votes for the 20 candidates with scanner confidence >= 0.5 (f001-f020), 1 vote for the other 40

findings.title: Catalog write endpoints (PUT/POST/DELETE) have no authentication or authorization
preconditions: Network reachability to the externally exposed mobile-bff YARP resource (AppHost.cs:62-63 uses WithExternalHttpEndpoints). This is the default deployment, not an extra condition.
Request includes a matching api-version query parameter (1.0, 1 or 2.0) to satisfy the YARP route match (Extensions.cs:97-105). The value is public and trivially guessable.
Target item id is known or guessable (integer, enumerable via the unauthenticated GET list endpoint). Only needed for PUT v2 and DELETE.
findings.threat_match: Privilege escalation to admin (anonymous caller reaches catalog-admin write functions). It does not touch the PII, PCI or tenant-leakage entries. No step raise is applied because severity is already HIGH.
findings.rationale:
The catalog write endpoints (CatalogApi.cs:100-117) have no authorization, and Catalog.API has no auth middleware. The externally exposed mobile-bff YARP resource (AppHost.cs:62-64) routes `/catalog-api/api/catalog/items` and `/items/{id}` (Extensions.cs:97,105) without method or auth restrictions, so anonymous PUT, POST and DELETE reach the service. UpdateItem (CatalogApi.cs:373-399) lets the caller change prices and publishes the price-change event.

An anonymous internet caller can create, modify or delete catalog items, including prices, through the public BFF with a single HTTP request. The only gates are a public api-version query string and an enumerable id, and no control mitigates this on the path. Strictly the "1-2 preconditions" rule would suggest MEDIUM, but the preconditions are trivial and non-restrictive, so they do not reduce exploitability. Impact is integrity and business-logic only (price manipulation, the price-change event, catalog destruction), with no PII/PCI exposure or code execution. The HIGH claim is defensible, though at the low end of HIGH.
first_links: src/eShop.AppHost/Extensions.cs (the /api/catalog/{*any} catch-all route in ConfigureMobileBffRoutes, line number not captured)
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Mike Kistler (3/11 recent commits); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Mobile BFF YARP routes have no HTTP method restriction, so unauthenticated catalog create/update/delete is reachable from the internet
preconditions: Attacker can reach the mobile-bff YARP proxy (external endpoint, AppHost.cs:62-64). This is the default exposure, not a real precondition.
Request includes a matching api-version query value (1.0, 1 or 2.0). Trivially attacker-supplied.
The route (Extensions.cs:142-143 catch-all, or the /items and /items/{id} routes) has no method restriction and no auth policy, so POST/PUT/DELETE are forwarded.
Catalog.API's mutation handlers have no authorization. This is f001, a separate finding, and it is the actual cause of the impact.
findings.threat_match: Privilege escalation to admin (anonymous caller performs admin-only catalog mutation). It is a loose match, so there is no uplift.
findings.rationale:
mobile-bff is externally exposed (AppHost.cs:62-64). Its catch-all /api/catalog/{*any} (Extensions.cs:142-143) and the specific /items and /items/{id} routes match any HTTP method, gated only by an api-version query value an attacker can supply. catalog-api's POST, PUT and DELETE handlers (CatalogApi.cs:100-114) have no authorization, and nothing in Catalog.API configures authentication. So an anonymous POST, PUT or DELETE reaches catalog mutation through the BFF.

The route config places no auth or method restriction on the externally exposed BFF, so an anonymous caller can forward POST/PUT/DELETE to catalog-api with only an attacker-controlled api-version query. Catalog-api is unauthenticated on its own (f001), so the proxy exposure is the path to it and neither finding is exploitable end to end without the other. The impact is anonymous tampering with or deletion of catalog data, which means integrity and availability loss of product data. There is no RCE, no PII or PCI exposure, and no tenant crossing. This is a duplicate or amplifier of f001, and counting it as a separate HIGH inflates the alert count slightly. The root-cause fix is auth in Catalog.API (f001); a BFF method allowlist is only defense in depth. I did not re-check CatalogApi.cs; that rests on the verifier's account and the routes in Extensions.cs, which I did read.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Eric Erhardt (6/13 recent commits); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: GetOrder returns any order by integer id with no ownership check
preconditions: Attacker holds a valid authenticated account (any registered user via identity-api); Ordering.API requires auth and the endpoint has no unauthenticated path.
Attacker reaches GET /api/orders/{orderId:int} through the external mobile-bff YARP route (AppHost Extensions.cs:146), or an internal position.
Attacker needs a valid integer order id. IDs come from the HiLo sequence "orderseq", so they are sequential and guessable by enumeration.
At least one other user's order must exist.
findings.threat_match: Tenant-to-tenant data leakage, and compliance-scoped PII exposure. Orders return street, city, state, country and zip, plus order contents. This match raises the result from the base tier by one step, but the base tier is itself capped at MEDIUM by the authenticated-access column, so the final label stays MEDIUM.
findings.rationale:
`OrdersApi.cs:80-84` passes only `orderId` to `OrderQueries.GetOrderAsync`, which filters only on `o.Id == id` (`OrderQueries.cs:10`). It returns the address, items and status (`OrderQueries.cs:20-26`). Authentication is required (`Program.cs:22`), but no buyer identity is compared, unlike `GetOrdersFromUserAsync` (`OrderQueries.cs:40`). The mobile-bff YARP route (`eShop.AppHost/Extensions.cs:146`) exposes it to external authenticated users. Any user can read other users' orders by iterating integer ids.

I read OrdersApi.cs and OrderQueries.cs. GetOrderAsync(int id) filters only on o.Id == id. The handler never reads the caller's identity, and the route is exposed to authenticated users. Any logged-in user can read any other customer's shipping address, order items and status by walking sequential ids. This is a classic BOLA, and the impact is a PII read with no write path. Under the derived rubric it is MEDIUM (authenticated, 1-2 preconditions, read-only). HIGH is slightly inflated: it needs an account, and it exposes no payment card data or unauthenticated access, though it is a real, trivially exploitable privacy leak that should be fixed.
first_links: src/Ordering.API/Apis/OrdersApi.cs (api.MapGet("{orderId:int}", GetOrderAsync) in the api/orders group; handler calls services.Queries.GetOrderAsync(orderId) with no user identity)
findings.owner_hint: top committers: Aditya Mandaleeka, Almar Aubel, Erin McLaughlin (1/4 each); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Any authenticated user can cancel any order by OrderNumber
preconditions: Attacker holds a valid authenticated session/JWT (any ordinary buyer account; self-registration on identity-api is presumably open)
Attacker supplies a valid x-requestid GUID (trivially self-generated)
Target order exists and is in a non-Paid/non-Shipped state (e.g. Submitted/AwaitingValidation/StockConfirmed); the integer order id is guessable/sequential
findings.threat_match: Tenant-to-tenant data leakage (cross-user object access; only loosely matches, since it is an integrity/availability impact rather than data disclosure). Not enough of a match to raise severity.
findings.rationale:
`PUT api/orders/cancel` (`OrdersApi.cs:11,22-41`) is reachable by any authenticated user via the Mobile BFF route `/api/orders/{*any}` (`AppHost/Extensions.cs:146`). The command carries only an attacker-controlled `OrderNumber`. `CancelOrderCommandHandler.cs:21-27` and `OrderRepository.GetAsync` (`OrderRepository.cs:21-23`) load by id with no buyer comparison. `Order.SetCancelledStatus` (`Order.cs:142-153`) refuses only Paid or Shipped orders, so any other user's pending order can be cancelled by iterating integer ids.

I read CancelOrderAsync and CancelOrderCommandHandler. The handler loads the order by the attacker-supplied OrderNumber and calls SetCancelledStatus with no buyer-ownership check, so this is a real BOLA/IDOR. Exploitation needs only a low-privilege authenticated user and sequential ids, so it falls at the authenticated/1-2 preconditions tier, which is MEDIUM. The impact is limited to cancelling other users' unshipped, unpaid orders (integrity/availability). It discloses no PII and gives no code execution or privilege escalation, so HIGH is a modest inflation.
first_links: src/Ordering.API/Apis/OrdersApi.cs:11 (`api.MapPut("/cancel", CancelOrderAsync)`), then OrdersApi.cs:22-41, then CancelOrderCommandHandler.cs:21-27.

findings.title: CreateOrder trusts UserId and UserName from the request body
preconditions: Attacker holds a valid authenticated session (any registered user) with a token accepted by Ordering.API, directly or via the mobile-bff proxy
Attacker knows the victim's sub/UserId (a GUID, not trivially guessable or enumerable)

Attacker sends POST /api/orders with a fresh x-requestid header and a body containing the victim's UserId and UserName; this works because the endpoint trusts body-supplied identity (OrdersApi.cs:141) with no comparison to the caller's claims
Attacker supplies their own payment card details, so the attacker pays for the forged order
findings.threat_match: Tenant-to-tenant data leakage (loosely; this is a cross-user integrity/write issue, not a read leak). It does not raise severity.
findings.rationale:
`CreateOrderAsync` copies `request.UserId` and `request.UserName` from the body into `CreateOrderCommand` (`OrdersApi.cs:141`) with no comparison to the caller's identity. The handler uses those values for the Order and the integration event (`CreateOrderCommandHandler.cs:32,40`), and `.RequireAuthorization()` (`Program.cs:22`) only enforces authentication. The externally exposed mobile-bff proxies `/api/orders/*` raw to this endpoint (`Extensions.cs:146`), so an authenticated user can submit another user's `UserId`. Impact is moderate: forged orders and a cleared basket for the victim, with the attacker's own card.

The identity-spoofing flaw is real. CreateOrderAsync takes UserId and UserName from the request body, and the handler uses them for the Order and the OrderStartedIntegrationEvent (CreateOrderCommandHandler.cs:32,40) without checking them against the caller's identity. An attacker can create orders under a victim's identity and trigger the basket-clear event for the victim. Exploitation needs authentication plus knowledge of a victim GUID. The impact is integrity-only: no data is read, the attacker pays with their own card, and the victim's basket is cleared. That puts it at MEDIUM, not HIGH. The threat-model match is weak because no data is exfiltrated, so there is no step up. I did not read the full Ordering.API request path beyond these snippets, so the verdict rests on the verifier's account and the code I read. [Likely 🟡]
findings.owner_hint: top committers: Aditya Mandaleeka, Chris Martinez, David Fowler (1/4 each); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Token signing key is a committed, publicly known RSA key (AddDeveloperSigningCredential loads tempkey.jwk)
preconditions: Deployed Identity.API actually loads the committed tempkey.jwk. Duende AddDeveloperSigningCredential() defaults to a "tempkey.jwk" file in the content root and generates one if it is absent. The csproj copies the committed file to the output (Content Include, CopyToOutputDirectory), so it is likely loaded, but this is unconfirmed.

The deployment runs this sample configuration unchanged (no production signing key swapped in, KeyManagement.Enabled=false, no override). Program.cs has no environment guard and TODO comments mark both lines as non-production.
The attacker has the repo (public sample) or the key file. No target access is needed to forge a token.
The downstream APIs validate tokens only by signature against Identity.API's JWKS (issuer and audience), with no extra binding. The verifier cited AuthenticationExtensions.cs:33-38 for this.
The attacker can send HTTP requests with a bearer token to an endpoint that is reachable, i.e. the BFF or webapp. Internal APIs are reached through the BFF.
findings.threat_match: Privilege escalation to admin and unauthenticated remote access. The forged-token impact (any subject or scope) maps to both. This raises severity by one step from the precondition-derived level.
findings.rationale:
Program.cs:37 calls AddDeveloperSigningCredential() with no arguments (default tempkey.jwk), and Program.cs:29 disables key management. src/Identity.API/tempkey.jwk is tracked in git and contains the private RSA parameter "D". Identity.API.csproj:50 copies it to the output directory, so a deployed service signs with a publicly known key. .gitignore only excludes wwwroot/lib/ and keys/, not tempkey.jwk. Downstream APIs trust the issuer's JWKS (src/eShop.ServiceDefaults/AuthenticationExtensions.cs:33-38), so anyone with the repo can forge tokens for any subject or scope. The TODO comments at Program.cs:28 and :36 mark this as sample code, which weakens the case (rules 3 and 13), but the key is committed and shipped, so the exploit is concrete for any deployment of this code. I did not confirm how the library resolves the default key file path (needs library source, outside the repo).

The access level is unauthenticated remote, but 3 or more preconditions must hold: the key file is loaded by the deployed server, the sample config is unchanged in the deployment, and the downstream APIs trust the JWKS alone. That count caps the derived severity at MEDIUM or LOW, and the threat-model match for privilege escalation raises it one step to MEDIUM. The impact is full token forgery if the key is loaded, which is serious, but this is an eShop reference sample with explicit "don't use in production" markers, so HIGH is inflated by one level. The verifier could not confirm the Duende default path resolution, so a runtime check is needed: compare the published JWKS kid from /.well-known/openid-configuration/jwks against the committed tempkey.jwk. If they match, this rises to HIGH for any real deployment.
findings.owner_hint: top committers: Aditya Mandaleeka, Brennan, Michael Stonis (1/3 each); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Ship endpoint is an admin-only action with no role or ownership check
preconditions: Attacker holds a registered, authenticated account (valid bearer token from identity-api). Self-registration is assumed, not checked.
The attacker knows or guesses the target order number. These are sequential integers, so guessing is cheap.
The target order must be in Paid status, which is a state-dependent window.
The ship endpoint must be proxied by the BFF. The verifier cites Extensions.cs:146 for this, and I did not re-check it.
findings.threat_match: Privilege escalation to admin (a normal user invokes the administrator-only ship action, a BFLA). Raised one step from LOW to MEDIUM.
findings.rationale:
`ShipOrderCommandHandler.cs:21-27` ships any order by number with no caller identity check. `Program.cs:21-22` applies only bare `RequireAuthorization()`, with no role or ownership policy in Ordering.API. The BFF route at `Extensions.cs:146` exposes `/api/orders/*` externally. Any registered user can therefore ship any `Paid` order. The impact is limited to business-state integrity, so medium rather than HIGH.

The authorization gap is real. Any logged-in user can ship another user's Paid order, because the code only calls bare RequireAuthorization() and checks no role or ownership. The precondition count (3-4, including the Paid-state window) and the authenticated access level put the base score at LOW. The privilege-escalation threat-model match raises it one step to MEDIUM. The impact is limited to business-state integrity: no data is exposed, there is no code execution, and the order can still be cancelled or corrected. HIGH is inflated for that reason, since it needs an authenticated attacker, a state-dependent window and has low impact. [Likely 🟡]
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Aditya Mandaleeka (1/1 recent commits); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Order line prices, discount and product names are taken from the client
preconditions: Attacker holds a valid authenticated account, e.g. self-registered via Identity.API with a bearer token. Ordering.API only calls RequireAuthorization.
The mobile-bff YARP route /api/orders/{*any} (eShop.AppHost/Extensions.cs:146) forwards to Ordering.API. I confirmed this route exists.

The attacker crafts a POST to api/orders with an x-requestid header and a CreateOrderRequest whose Items carry attacker-chosen UnitPrice and Discount. The request needs a card number of at least 4 characters.

The order's downstream effect is only a tampered total. CreateOrderCommandHandler copies the items into the order unchecked. Payment is a stub (a config flag), so nothing charges the wrong amount. A real loss needs a fulfillment or financial process that trusts the stored price. I did not verify that process.
findings.rationale:
The mobile BFF route `/api/orders/{*any}` (src/eShop.AppHost/Extensions.cs:146) reaches Ordering.API, which only requires authorization (Program.cs:22). `CreateOrderAsync` (OrdersApi.cs:141) forwards client-supplied items. CreateOrderCommandHandler.cs:44 copies UnitPrice and Discount into the order with no Catalog or basket check. An authenticated user can therefore order at a tampered price. `UserId` is also client-supplied, which is a related issue. Rule 3 is arguable because this is upstream demo-app design, so I rate it a moderate true positive.

A low-privilege authenticated user can submit an order with arbitrary prices through the externally exposed BFF route, and the handler has no catalog or basket re-pricing, so the flaw is real. It requires authentication, and the impact is limited to financial integrity of one's own order. The shipped payment processor is a stub, so there is no direct monetary loss here. It does not match any operator threat-model entry, so there is no uplift. HIGH is inflated by one level; MEDIUM fits.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Aditya Mandaleeka (1/1 recent commits); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Seeded accounts alice and bob with fixed known password "Pass123$" are created on every startup
preconditions: The Identity.API seeder runs (it does on every startup; Program.cs:12 has no environment gate), and the deployment keeps the seeded alice/bob rows and does not change their passwords.
Attacker can reach the Identity.API login endpoint over HTTP (external endpoint in the AppHost).
Attacker knows the usernames and the fixed password "Pass123$". These are public in the open-source sample repo.
The login succeeds as a standard customer account, with no admin role. The impact is limited to those two accounts' own data.
findings.threat_match: Compliance-scoped data exposure (PII/PCI), weak match. The seeded users hold name, address, phone and a masked card number (XXXXXXXXXXXX1881) with the CVV "123", and this is only the two demo accounts' own data. It does not match the privilege-escalation, RCE or tenant-leak entries. No severity bump applied.
findings.rationale:
Program.cs:12 registers UsersSeed with no environment check, and MigrateDbContextExtensions.cs:23-46 runs it on every startup. UsersSeed.cs:33 and :78 create alice and bob with the fixed password "Pass123$". Identity.API is external, so the known credentials give a working login. The sample-app "intended design" argument is the main doubt.

Anyone can log in as alice or bob using the public default credentials. This is a real default-credential issue, but it only gives a standard-user session on two demo accounts whose card data is masked and whose PII is fictional. It is the eShop reference sample's deliberate demo seed, and the code comment in Program.cs already says the migration approach is not for production. The exposure only matters if the sample is deployed as-is, so MEDIUM is the upper bound and LOW is defensible. The claimed MEDIUM is slightly inflated.
findings.owner_hint: top committers: Aditya Mandaleeka, Rob Conery, toyzoz (1/3 each); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: BFF /api/orders/{*any} catch-all exposes all ordering write routes (ship, cancel) with no method limits or role check
preconditions: Attacker holds a valid logged-in account (self-registered via identity-api) and a bearer token accepted by Ordering.API
Request carries api-version=1.0 or 1 (the route's query-parameter match), sent to the external mobile-bff /api/orders/{*any} route
Ordering.API's own missing role/ownership checks (f007/f008) must be what permits the abuse. The BFF route adds no new capability beyond forwarding
findings.threat_match: Privilege escalation to admin (weak match, via f007/f008 on ship/cancel); no match for the BFF route itself
findings.rationale:
The external mobile-bff catch-all at Extensions.cs:146 forwards every HTTP method to ordering-api. Ordering.API only requires authentication (Program.cs:21-22), so any logged-in user can invoke the ship and cancel routes (OrdersApi.cs:11-12). Ship is a back-office operation that the BFF exposes with no role or method limit.

The catch-all at Extensions.cs:146 does forward PUT /ship and /cancel (OrdersApi.cs:11-12) to the internet, and I confirmed it is scoped only by an api-version query match, so it is reachable by any authenticated user. But a YARP route is a transparent proxy to an API that is meant to be consumed. The defect is the absent role and ownership authorization in Ordering.API, already tracked as f007/f008. This finding is an exposure amplifier of those, not an independent flaw, so it should be merged into them or at most carry MEDIUM. Claimed MEDIUM is slightly inflated as a standalone item because fixing the route alone (for example allow-listing paths) would be defense-in-depth, not the root fix.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Eric Erhardt (6/13 recent commits); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Cross-tenant disclosure: order events are sent to every user's subscriptions, not just the order owner's
preconditions: Attacker must reach webhooks-api over the network. AppHost.cs:56-59 has no WithExternalHttpEndpoints. The mobile-bff has no route to it, and neither does webapp. The WebhookClient app (AppHost.cs:67-69) is also not marked external. So this needs a position on the internal network, or a deployment that exposes webhooks-api. [Certain 🟢]
Attacker needs a valid identity-api token (RequireAuthorization). Any registered user qualifies, so no admin role is needed. [Certain 🟢]
Attacker must POST a subscription for the Shipped and/or Paid event type. The grant-URL check can be satisfied with an attacker-controlled endpoint. [Likely 🟡]
Attacker must host a listener for the callback URL. Other users' orders must also reach Shipped or Paid, and the data is only delivered after that happens. [Likely 🟡]
findings.threat_match: Tenant-to-tenant data leakage (cross-user PII and order data via subscriptions that are not filtered by user). It matches only loosely, because the exposure is limited and the service is internal.
findings.rationale:
A registered subscriber gets every user's Shipped and Paid event, because WebhooksRetriever.cs filters by event type only and WebhooksSender.SendAll POSTs the whole payload. Registration requires only authentication (Program.cs .RequireAuthorization(), WebHooksApi.cs POST). The grant-URL check is satisfied by an attacker-controlled endpoint, and AppHost.cs:63 exposes the service externally. The leaked data is order IDs, buyer names and, for Paid, items, so impact is moderate. The claim that the Shipped event carries items is wrong.

The flaw is real: WebhooksRetriever filters by event type only, so any subscriber receives every user's Shipped and Paid events. The leaked data is order IDs, buyer names and Paid items. However, webhooks-api is not an external endpoint in the AppHost, and I found no webapp or BFF path to it. Reaching it therefore needs an internal foothold or a non-default exposure, which gives 3 or more preconditions and LOW. A threat-model match could lift this one step to MEDIUM if webhooks-api is exposed in a real deployment, but under the AppHost as written, MEDIUM is somewhat inflated. Confirming the real deployment topology needs a manual check. [Likely 🟡]

findings.title: Chatbot renders model-controlled markdown images as raw MarkupString with attacker-chosen external src, enabling zero-click exfiltration
findings.category: Improper output handling / data exfiltration via LLM output (indirect prompt injection)
findings.rationale: `Chatbot.razor:46` passes model/user text to `MessageProcessor.AllowImages` (`MessageProcessor.cs:24`). That method encodes `src` and `title`, but allows any external image URL, and there is no CSP in WebApp. Exploitation needs prompt injection, and the only reachable prompt source for an external attacker is the victim's own chat input. The catalog, the other injection vector, is written only through the internal Catalog.API (`CatalogApi.cs:100-114`), so reaching it requires an internal compromise. That makes this an LLM-prompt-input hardening gap, not a concrete exploit.

findings.title: SSRF via webhook Url/GrantUrl: OPTIONS grant check and later POSTs to any attacker-chosen host, including internal addresses
findings.rationale: Webhooks.API has no external endpoint in `AppHost.cs:56-58`, and the BFF does not route to it (`AppHost.cs:62-64`). It also requires authorization (`Program.cs:21`). Registering a user-supplied callback URL is the feature's intended design, and the response is blind (only 201 or 400). The missing private-IP blocking in `GrantUrlTesterService.cs:7-27` is a hardening gap that matters only after a service compromise or if the service is later exposed.

findings.title: JWT audience validation disabled and no scope or policy enforcement, so any token from the issuer is accepted by Basket, Ordering and Webhooks
findings.rationale: `ValidateAudience=false` at AuthenticationExtensions.cs:49 is real, but issuer validation remains (lines 38-46). The main clients (webapp, maui) are already granted orders, basket and webhooks scopes together (Config.cs:59-68, 99-108), so audience checks would not restrict them. Only the narrow swagger clients differ, and their tokens are for the user's own `sub`, so no privilege or data boundary is crossed. The APIs are internal and need a valid issuer token, so this is hardening-only with no concrete exploit.

findings.title: Unauthenticated broker messages drive order payment state transitions (forged StockConfirmed / PaymentSucceeded / PaymentFailed)
findings.rationale: The RabbitMQ broker is an internal Aspire resource (src/eShop.AppHost/AppHost.cs:10) and is not an external endpoint. It is only referenced by backend services (AppHost.cs:34-77). Forging events needs broker credentials or a compromised service, which is outside the untrusted-HTTP threat model. Trusting messages on the internal bus is the design of RabbitMQEventBus.cs:132+. Adding message authentication would be missing hardening with no concrete exploit from an untrusted source (exclusion 13).
first_links: src/EventBusRabbitMQ/RabbitMQEventBus.cs:156 (routing key and body taken from the delivery, only reachable by a broker publisher)

findings.title: Full card number, CVV (card_security_number), expiry and holder name are issued as claims without scope filtering
findings.rationale: ProfileService.cs:23 does issue unfiltered claims, and Config.cs:72 forces them into ID tokens. But the only values ever stored come from UsersSeed.cs (masked demo card numbers and dummy CVVs), and no code path stores real card data on `ApplicationUser`. The claims are the user's own data in the eShop reference app's design, so there is no concrete exploit.

findings.title: Webhook token validation is disabled by default because ValidateToken is read from the wrong config key
findings.rationale: The key mismatch is genuine, so validation is off by default. But `webhooksclient` is not exposed externally in AppHost.cs:67-69 and nothing in the BFF routes reaches it. A forged payload only adds a row that auto-escaped Blazor renders, so this is missing hardening in an internal demo service with no concrete exploit.

findings.title: UpdateItem copies every client-supplied field onto the entity, including PictureFileName, stock and OnReorder
findings.rationale: The over-posting only matters because the endpoint is unauthenticated, and that is already covered by the missing-auth finding. The "replace the whole item" behaviour (CatalogApi.cs:100-109, UpdateItem at 365) is intended, and price is already writable. I found no concrete exploit from PictureFileName, OnReorder or a client-chosen Id.

findings.title: CVV and cardholder data logged in clear via structured command logging
findings.rationale: The command is logged with {@Command} at LoggingBehavior.cs:9, and OrdersApi.cs:134 does the same for the raw request. No structured-logging library that destructures objects is present, so default MEL likely prints only the type name. The CVV (CreateOrderCommand.cs:53) is not demonstrably emitted. The remaining risk is hardening-only.

findings.title: LLM tools run with the user's identity and no confirmation; untrusted catalog text can drive AddToCart and PII disclosure
findings.category: Excessive agency / prompt injection tool abuse
findings.rationale: This is generic LLM prompt injection. The tools act only within the user's own identity and scope (ChatState.cs:96-111, 137-143), with no cross-user impact and no exfiltration channel. The unauthenticated catalog writes (CatalogApi.cs:100-114) are on an internal service, so poisoning needs a prior compromise.

findings.title: Forged OrderStarted event deletes any user's basket by event UserId
findings.rationale: The handler at OrderStartedIntegrationEventHandler.cs:14 trusts the event's UserId, but the only producer (CreateOrderCommandHandler.cs:32) sets it from the order command. Exploiting it needs write access to the internal RabbitMQ broker, which is already a compromise. The result is a low-impact nuisance, a deleted basket.

findings.title: Forged or replayed OrderStatusChangedToPaid event decrements arbitrary catalog stock, non-idempotently
findings.category: business logic / replay / unvalidated event fields
findings.rationale: The handler (lines 13-18) decrements stock without dedup, as claimed. The event is published only by Ordering.API after payment, over an internal RabbitMQ broker that identity-api, webapp and mobile-bff don't expose. Forging it needs a broker compromise, which is out of scope as a post-compromise state. The replay claim rests on theoretical at-least-once duplicate delivery with minor stock-count effect. The comment at line 12 shows the design intent. Caveat: my grep for other publishers failed, so I did not verify that no other service publishes this event.

findings.title: Custom-scheme redirect (maui://authcallback) on an exported activity is hijackable and has no verified-link protection
findings.rationale: PKCE is enforced for the maui client (Identity.API/Configuration/Config.cs:56), so an intercepted code cannot be redeemed without the verifier. The exported activity (WebAuthenticationCallbackActivity.cs:6) is required for the redirect. What remains is custom-scheme hardening only.

findings.title: Handler exceptions are swallowed and the message is Acked, so failures drop events and leave orders in inconsistent states, with no DLX
findings.category: poison message handling / lost events (threat T15)
findings.rationale: The ack-on-failure is documented as intentional at RabbitMQEventBus.cs:177-179. It only loses events when a handler fails, and no external attacker path to a handler failure was found. This is a missing dead-letter exchange, a hardening and reliability gap with no concrete exploit (exclusions 3 and 13).

findings.title: Weak OIDC client settings: shared secret "secret" on all confidential clients, webapp RequirePkce=false, implicit-flow swagger clients, secret on a public native client
findings.rationale: As above, with file:line citations. A known secret is useless without a stolen authorization code, and codes go only to the fixed registered redirect URIs. The missing PKCE on webapp and the implicit Swagger clients are hardening items or intended design, with no concrete exploit.

findings.title: Request-id marker is global, committed before processing, and failures are swallowed as success or null
findings.rationale: The request id is a random Guid chosen by the client. An attacker cannot guess a victim's id to burn it, and the Guid primary key on `ClientRequest` (`RequestManager.cs:25-37`) makes a double run fail the second insert. Swallowing exceptions after the marker is committed (`IdentifiedCommandHandler.cs:48,99-102`) is a reliability bug that only affects the caller's own retry.

findings.title: Non-constant-time token comparison, token logged in cleartext, and /check echoes the token header
findings.rationale: See the four points above. The token is a sample value, the echo is the design, and there is no concrete exploit path.

findings.title: BFF exposes the entire Identity.API app under /identity/* (all methods, no filtering)
findings.rationale: identity-api already has external HTTP endpoints at AppHost.cs:25-26, so the BFF proxy route at Extensions.cs:150-151 exposes no additional surface. It is a deliberate single-ingress convenience for mobile clients, and no concrete exploit is shown.

findings.title: UpdateBasket persists unvalidated ProductId and Quantity, and the model's validation is never invoked
findings.rationale: The basket is keyed by the caller's identity (BasketService.cs:38). Negative and zero quantities are rejected at order creation by OrderItem.cs:25-27, so they never reach order totals. The only remaining effect is a skewed total on the user's own cart page (CartPage.razor:123). That is hardening-only, with no concrete exploit shown.

findings.title: Whole-batch dispatch failure and unvalidated DestUrl scheme (only well-formedness checked)
findings.rationale: `WebHooksApi.cs:41` calls `TestGrantUrl`. At `GrantUrlTesterService.cs` `CheckSameOrigin` enforces same scheme, host and port, with an OPTIONS and token handshake. This is origin-level ownership proof by design, so a different path on the same origin gives no extra capability. `WebhooksSender.cs` starts all sends before `Task.WhenAll`, so a failure is only a nuisance.

findings.title: Webhook secret token logged in plaintext
findings.rationale: The log lines at GrantUrlTesterService.cs:17 and :25 exist as described. The token is subscriber-supplied (WebHooksApi.cs:41), and reading it needs log access, which is an operator privilege. The impact is forging deliveries to one receiver, with no external attack path. That makes it missing hardening only.

findings.title: Cleartext traffic globally enabled on Android, ATS disabled on MacCatalyst (ClientApp and HybridApp), and Android backup allowed
findings.rationale: The `networkSecurityConfig` attribute at AndroidManifest.xml:3 overrides `usesCleartextTraffic`. Resources/xml/network_security_config.xml permits cleartext only for 10.0.2.2, so the claim of global cleartext is wrong. The remaining items (`allowBackup`, ATS) are hardening-only mobile client settings with no concrete exploit, which falls under exclusions 13 and 9.

findings.title: Bearer token sent to user-editable gateway and identity URLs with no host allowlist or HTTPS enforcement
findings.rationale: See the summary above. The Preferences-backed endpoint setters (SettingsService.cs:97-124) are written only by the user's own Settings UI (SettingsView.xaml:126). The bearer attachment at RequestProvider.cs:116 is real but needs the user to point the app at an attacker host themselves.

findings.title: Trace-context header extraction runs outside the try/catch and throws on missing or non-byte[] headers, which can wedge the consumer
findings.category: input validation / null dereference in trace-context extraction (consumer DoS)
findings.rationale: The null and cast issue at lines 136-139 is real, but triggering it needs a malformed message published to the internal broker, which already means compromise. The OpenTelemetry propagator likely catches getter exceptions at line 145 (from memory, not checked). If it doesn't, the impact is one unacked message, which is a missing-hardening nuisance with no concrete exploit.

findings.title: returnUrl validation relies on Uri.IsAbsoluteUri and is passed to Nav.NavigateTo unchanged
findings.category: Open redirect (only relevant to token theft if chained)
findings.rationale: The open redirect at LogIn.razor:13-15 likely works with a crafted `returnUrl` such as `/\evil.com`. It is gated by `[Authorize]` and leaks no token, so the impact is phishing only. Open redirect is explicitly low-impact under rule 12.

findings.title: WebApp and Webhooks handlers trust event BuyerIdentityGuid and event contents: spoofed notifications and forged webhook payloads
findings.rationale: Handler at line 13 trusts the event, as claimed, but forging requires broker access (internal-only, post-compromise); trusting the internal bus is intended design and impact is low (spurious UI notification / webhook payload). Webhooks.API OrderStatusChangedToPaidIntegrationEventHandler.cs builds WebhookData from @event unchanged, again only reachable via the broker.

findings.title: User-controlled Token written to HTTP header without validation
findings.rationale: The registration endpoint (WebHooksApi.cs:41) calls TestGrantUrl, which adds the same header unguarded at GrantUrlTesterService.cs:21. An invalid token throws there and is never persisted, so the sender never sees one. The header-splitting risk is also blocked by .NET header validation.

findings.title: Forwarded headers enabled on every project with no trusted proxy restriction
findings.rationale: Extensions.cs:36 only sets the env var, the standard Aspire proxy configuration. Without a cache, reset-email flow or other cross-user consumer, a spoofed X-Forwarded-Host only changes the attacker's own response. `IssuerUri` is commented out at Identity.API/Program.cs:20. This is missing hardening with no concrete exploit.

findings.title: Authentication silently not registered when the "Identity" config section is missing
findings.rationale: See above. The early return at `AuthenticationExtensions.cs:24-28` needs a missing config section. `AppHost.cs:35,46,59` sets `Identity__Url`, and the other services' `.RequireAuthorization()` calls suggest a startup failure rather than open access.

findings.title: Manual-only authorization: [AllowAnonymous] on GetBasket, and no [Authorize] or fallback policy on the other RPCs
findings.rationale: Every RPC derives the user id solely from the token `sub` claim and rejects or returns empty when it is absent (BasketService.cs:16,39,62). There is no client-supplied id, so no IDOR and no unauthenticated access to data. The scanner itself concedes the behavior is safe, leaving only a hardening suggestion.

findings.title: User search text is sent to a third-party embedding model without a length limit, and is logged at Trace and Debug level
findings.rationale: The first call-site I read is CatalogApi.cs:300, where GetItemsBySemanticRelevance passes the text to GetEmbeddingAsync. The Trace log at CatalogAI.cs:64-66 records only the caller's own input in internal logs and is off by default. The cost-abuse claim is volumetric DoS (exclusion 1). Dropping the Trace/Debug logging of search text would only be hardening (exclusion 13).

findings.title: Logout/refresh-token handling is weak; refresh token is never revoked at the IdP
findings.rationale: SignOutAsync calls LogoutAsync (IdentityService.cs:47), which hits the end-session endpoint, then clears tokens at line 54. The claim that it only clears local storage is wrong. Only explicit refresh-token revocation is absent, which is hardening that needs prior device compromise, with no concrete exploit shown.

findings.title: Automatic migration and seeding at startup, with default Postgres credential in appsettings.Development.json
findings.rationale: Startup migration is documented as dev-oriented design (Program.cs:9-12) and has no attacker-reachable trigger. The Postgres password in appsettings.Development.json:3 is under a key the code does not read (Program.cs:7 uses "identitydb" via Aspire, AppHost.cs:12-18). It is a localhost dev value, and it overlaps f018. Only missing hardening remains.

findings.title: Logout without prompt via GET, enabling forced logout from third-party pages
findings.rationale: AccountOptions.cs:12 sets ShowLogoutPrompt to false, so the GET Logout at AccountController.cs:152-156 signs the user out without an anti-forgery check. The attacker gains nothing beyond forcing a logout, and rule 12 names CSRF on logout as a low-impact nuisance. The behavior is also the default IdentityServer quickstart design.

findings.title: Diagnostics page gates on RemoteIpAddress, which is unreliable behind a reverse proxy; it exposes the authenticated user's claims and tokens
findings.rationale: DiagnosticsController.cs:13-17 gates on RemoteIpAddress, and Identity.API does not enable forwarded headers, so the check sees the real peer. A bypass needs a same-host proxy, which is speculative. The page returns only the caller's own authenticated claims and tokens (DiagnosticsController.cs:19), so there is no cross-user disclosure. Without a concrete exploit this is missing-hardening only.

findings.title: Committed DB superuser password "yourWeak(!)Password" in Development appsettings of 5 services, which are activated by committed launch profiles
findings.rationale: The password sits in a Development-only appsettings file that points at localhost. Aspire overrides it in orchestrated runs (src/eShop.AppHost/AppHost.cs:12), and production does not load it. It is a local-dev fixture with no concrete exploit.

findings.title: GetOrder swallows all exceptions as 404, and the draft endpoint exposes the builder with no buyer binding
findings.rationale: The bare catch at OrdersApi.cs:87-90 turns a missing order (KeyNotFoundException, OrderQueries.cs:6-13) into a 404, so error mapping is the intended behavior. The draft endpoint at OrdersApi.cs:106-116 persists nothing, so the supplied BuyerId gives an attacker nothing to exploit. The real IDOR in GetOrderAsync (OrderQueries.cs:6-10) is a different issue that the scanner did not report.

findings.title: The card number column is stored without encryption, and only the masked PAN is persisted. The CVV has no column mapping.
findings.rationale: OrdersApi.cs:140-144 masks the PAN before it reaches the command handler, so the stored value is already `XXXX…last4`. CreateOrderCommandHandler.cs:40 persists whatever the command carries, and that is the masked value. The CVV is not mapped to any column. The only residual risk is a hypothetical future caller that skips masking, which is a missing-hardening concern with no concrete exploit.

findings.title: PaymentProcessor does not charge anything and responds to a StockConfirmed event with OrderId only, with no amount, buyer or state verification
findings.category: business logic / payment bypass by design
findings.rationale: The handler's own comment (lines 15-19) says it simulates a payment gateway and uses a configuration value in place of a real payment. Lines 21-28 branch only on options.CurrentValue.PaymentSucceeded. This is documented demo behavior, not an unintended bypass. The handler subscribes to an internal event bus, so an external attacker cannot reach it, and the option is an operator-controlled setting. I did not read the Ordering handler or trace the bus subscription. The claim that result events carry only the OrderId describes an incomplete simulation, not a concrete exploit. The scanner itself rates it LOW and shows no attacker path. [Certain 🟢]

findings.title: Unauthenticated MapForwarder for /product-images/{id} with an unconstrained id substituted into the catalog-api path
findings.category: SSRF / path injection (low) and unauthenticated proxy
findings.rationale: A single route segment cannot inject slashes, so the id cannot reach other catalog routes. The reachable endpoints are public GET catalog data. The finding is missing-hardening only (src/WebApp/Program.cs:32; src/Catalog.API/Apis/CatalogApi.cs:37,47,105,114).

findings.title: Logout is anonymous-callable and does no redirect, so the OIDC sign-out is not completed
findings.rationale: Logout is anonymous-callable and has no redirect, but the antiforgery check (AuthenticationEndpoints.cs:14) stops CSRF and an anonymous caller has no session to end. No exploit exists, only a missing hardening or UX detail.

findings.title: Postgres uses unpinned third-party image ankane/pgvector:latest, and all databases share a single superuser
findings.rationale: AppHost.cs:12-15 is operator-controlled orchestration config, not reachable by an external attacker. The unpinned image tag and shared Postgres server are intended Aspire reference-app design. The finding describes missing hardening with no concrete exploit path.

findings.title: ESHOP_USE_HTTP_ENDPOINTS toggle switches Identity, webapp and webhooks clients to plain-HTTP launch profiles, combined with RequireHttpsMetadata=false
findings.rationale: The toggle is a documented CI/test-only switch (AppHost.cs:108-112) set in `.github/workflows/playwright.yml:36`. It needs operator-level environment control and gives an external attacker no concrete exploit. It is also missing-hardening-only, with no demonstrated path.

findings.title: Auth token handler attaches the user's access token to every outgoing request from the client, with no host allow-list
findings.rationale: The handler (HttpClientExtensions.cs:44) sets the Authorization header without checking the destination host. Every registration (WebApp Extensions.cs:30-40, WebhookClient Extensions.cs:19-21) uses a fixed internal service-discovery base address, and the callers I read use only relative paths. No attacker-controlled host reaches these clients, so this is hardening-only.

findings.title: OpenAPI document endpoint mapped in all environments when the OpenApi config section exists
findings.rationale: OpenApi.Extensions.cs:24 maps the OpenAPI document with no environment gate, as claimed. The affected services (Catalog, Ordering, Webhooks) are internal, and the document only describes endpoints and scopes, which is not sensitive. No concrete exploit follows from it, so it is a hardening-only item.

findings.title: Handler logs the entire integration event object, including the user id, at Information level
findings.rationale: The event record has only UserId plus the base Id and CreationDate (Events/OrderStartedIntegrationEvent.cs:6). No PII, credentials or tokens are logged, and the user id is already logged at line 12 and used at line 14. There is no concrete exploit, only low-impact logging.

findings.title: Debug-only certificate validation relaxation (trusts any cert whose Issuer is CN=localhost)
findings.rationale: The relaxation sits inside `#if DEBUG` (MauiProgram.cs:118-147) and exists to trust a local `CN=localhost` dev certificate. The Android callback otherwise defers to standard validation (line 132), and iOS trusts only `https://localhost` URLs (line 138). Release builds get a null handler (MauiProgram.cs:81-82, 89-90). This is missing-hardening with no concrete exploit.

findings.title: RedirectService.ExtractRedirectUriFromReturnUrl parses the redirect_uri by string splitting, but it appears unused
findings.rationale: The only callers are the DI registration (Program.cs:41) and a unit test (IdentityConfigurationTests.cs:49). No production code resolves IRedirectService or calls the method, so a crafted returnUrl cannot reach it. This is dead code with no exploit path. Earlier code-review text (THREAT_MODEL.md:77) mentions it, but I found no actual use.

findings.title: Outbox deserialization resolves types by name from a DB column, but only against a whitelist of entry-assembly types
findings.category: unsafe reflection / type resolution (reviewed, low risk)
findings.rationale: IntegrationEventLogService.cs:13-16,28 matches only a short name against entry-assembly types ending in "IntegrationEvent". It uses no Type.GetType, and IntegrationEventLogEntry.cs:15 sets EventTypeName from `@event.GetType().FullName`. Only the service writes the outbox rows, so exploiting this needs direct DB write access, which already gives the attacker much more. The scanner concedes there is no gadget. An unknown name gives null from FirstOrDefault, which fails safely. This is a hardening note with no concrete exploit.

findings.title: CheckoutAsync sends a hardcoded test card and ignores the user-submitted BasketCheckoutInfo card fields
findings.category: Sensitive data handling / hardcoded payment data
findings.rationale: `BasketState.cs:100-103` hardcodes a demo card. This is the eShop sample's placeholder payment, and the form (`Checkout.razor:11-50`) collects no card data. `Buyer` is set from authenticated `buyerId` at line 85 and 105, so there is no spoofing and no real-world exploit.
